generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, the active design of learning is easy to see. A statistics seminar is built around working through a dataset, not watching one being analysed; a research-methods workshop has you critique a study rather than hear it summarised. Tutors set these up from the intended learning outcomes, so when a psychology session asks you to apply or evaluate, the activity is there for you to do exactly that.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students see the same research-methods tutorial on their timetable, with a pre-task: read one study and come ready to argue whether its design supports its claim.

Tom reads the study and highlights the main findings to revise later. In the tutorial, Tom waits to be told what the study means. The session is built around a critique, but Tom has prepared as if it were a lecture, so there is little to contribute. This treats an active design as a passive one.

Amara notices the pre-task is asking for a judgement, so prepares one: the claim, the sample and method it rests on, and a reason the design might be questioned. In the tutorial, Amara joins the critique straight away. By reading the design of the session, Amara arrived able to do the very thing it was built for.

Both students did the reading. Only Amara worked out what the session was designed to make them do, and prepared for that.
generatedProse.summary: University learning in psychology is designed to be active: statistics by doing statistics, methods by critiquing studies. Most of it is constructivist, with some behaviourist, process-driven training such as learning a software package. Tutors design backwards from intended learning outcomes, so each activity has a purpose you can see. You can now tell active design from passive, explain constructive alignment, and work out how to engage with a psychology session on its own terms. The next lesson turns to how your work is judged.

check.body: A psychology tutor sets the outcome 'by the end you will be able to evaluate a study's methodology' before planning the tutorial. Why decide the outcome first?

items.text: So the activities and content can be built to lead you to that outcome (constructive alignment).
Because the outcome is a formality recorded after the class.
So the tutorial can cover as many studies as possible.
Because the reading must be chosen before anyone knows its purpose.

feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding the outcome first lets the tutor align the tutorial's activities and reading to it, which is constructive alignment.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the outcome is for in the design of the tutorial.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The outcome is set first so the activities and reading can be aligned to lead you to it. This backward design is constructive alignment.
